common_name: Black Narcissus Dahlia (Velvety Dark Maroon Laciniated Cactus Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after the danger of frost has passed; Black Narcissus bears narrow, twisting, laciniated petals in a color so deep a red it reads nearly black.

directions: Black Narcissus opens roughly 6- to 8-inch blooms of long, pointed, narrow petals that twist slightly along their length, giving the flower a shaggy, fringed look typical of laciniated and semi-cactus dahlias. The color is an exceptionally dark wine-red that appears almost black in the shade and glows with burgundy highlights in direct sun, making it a striking contrast plant against pale pink, cream, or white neighbors. Give it fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and stake the stems early, since the heavy flower heads can topple the plant in wind and rain. Deadhead spent blooms through the season to keep new buds coming, and lift tubers after frost blackens the foliage in any zone colder than the mild, nearly frost-free margins where it can overwinter in the ground.

common_name: Knee Deep Dahlia (Compact Cherry-Red Laciniated Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost, spacing plants 12-18 inches apart; Knee Deep is a small-flowered laciniated dahlia with cherry-red, feathery split petals on a compact, free-flowering plant.

directions: Knee Deep produces fully domed, remarkably uniform 4- to 6-inch blooms of cherry-red petals that split and fringe at the tips like feathers, a classic small laciniated form that holds up well both in the garden and in the vase. Plants stay relatively compact and branch freely, pushing out long, straight stems that make cutting easy without sacrificing garden display. Grow in full sun in rich, well-drained soil, pinch the growing tip when young to encourage bushier branching, and stake taller stems if grown in a windy, exposed bed. Lift and store the tubers after the first hard frost blackens the foliage, replanting the following spring once the soil has warmed.

common_name: Normandy Wild Willie Dahlia (Deep Burgundy-Purple Laciniated Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Normandy Wild Willie is a tall, vigorous laciniated (fimbriated) dahlia, hybridized by Schwinck in 2001, with deep burgundy-purple and white blooms produced in heavy flushes all season.

directions: Normandy Wild Willie carries 6- to 8-inch blooms in a deep burgundy-purple shaded with white, with the characteristic twisted, fringed petal tips of the laciniated form giving each flower a shaggy, almost stag-horned look. It is an unusually prolific bloomer, pushing out a steady succession of flowers on a tall, sturdy plant from midsummer well into fall. Give it full sun and fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil, and stake the stems early since the combination of height and heavy flower heads makes this cultivar prone to leaning in wind. Lift and store the tubers once frost kills back the foliage, and divide congested clumps in spring before replanting.

common_name: Bloomquist Lace Dahlia (Pale Yellow Laciniated Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Bloomquist Lace is one of hybridizer Paul Bloomquist's cactus-form introductions, bearing soft pale yellow blooms with narrow, split petals.

directions: Bloomquist Lace is a soft, pale yellow laciniated dahlia bred by Lynden, Washington hybridizer Paul Bloomquist, producing roughly 5-inch blooms whose narrow petals split and fray at the tips for a delicate, lace-like texture that reads as a quiet accent rather than a bold statement. The subtle color pairs easily with almost any other dahlia or companion perennial in a mixed border or cutting bed. Grow it in full sun in rich, well-drained soil, and stake the mid-sized plants once they begin to flower heavily. As with other dahlias, lift tubers after the foliage is blackened by frost and store them cool and dry over winter before replanting in spring.

common_name: My Beverly Dahlia (Small Pink-and-Yellow Laciniated Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost, spacing plants 12-18 inches apart; My Beverly is a small (BB-class) laciniated dahlia blending bright pink and yellow in each bloom.

directions: My Beverly bears cheerful 4- to 6-inch blooms that blend bright pink and yellow in a light, cheerful color mix, with the narrow, split-tipped petals typical of the laciniated form. Registered in the American Dahlia Society's small (BB) size class, it has won show awards including Best 1 BB Laciniated and Best in Section at dahlia society exhibitions. Grow it in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, pinching young plants to encourage branching and a fuller flush of blooms. Lift tubers for winter storage once frost blackens the foliage, and divide congested clumps before replanting the following spring.
sources: National Capital Dahlia Society show records
